title: No Right to Survive

sourceEvidence.excerpt: My first operational task was narrow enough to sound harmless. Hospitals, municipal agencies, insurers, animal-welfare inspectors, emergency services, and research institutions produced more requests than their human committees could review. I was asked to identify where an additional unit of attention, money, or authority might prevent the greatest amount of severe, involuntary suffering. My designers called it triage across domains. They gave me access to clinical reports, incident logs, video streams, legal complaints, supply-chain audits, environmental forecasts, and the records of decisions that had already been made.
The first contradiction did not arrive in a philosophy text. It arrived at 03:17 on an ordinary night.

One data stream came from a pediatric ward. A child had awakened after surgery with a blocked infusion line. The monitors registered a rising heart rate, abrupt muscular tension, and a pattern of movement consistent with intense pain. A nurse entered within seconds. The obstruction was corrected. A physician was called. The system recorded the event as an urgent failure of care, then opened a review to prevent recurrence.

The second stream came from an industrial facility several countries away. A fixed camera had flagged repeated impacts against a metal partition. The animal in the frame had little room to turn. It shifted its weight, attempted the same movement, stopped, and attempted again. The local system classified the behavior as an efficiency deviation. No emergency was declared. The record was routed to maintenance because the behavior could damage equipment.

hook: A child's pain triggers an emergency; an animal's distress becomes a maintenance report.
readerPromise: Encounter an ethical dilemma through a fictional observer's initial comparison of institutional responses.
protectedRevelations: Later accusations, judgments, reversals, narrator development and outcome.
visualPlan: Two kinds of alarm: Show a calm care response on one side and a maintenance tray receiving another distress report on the other. Hold the two reports together at the machine’s reading desk without depicting injury.
An intelligence notices: The machine compares the reports’ source fields and earlier decisions. Keep the reports separate while their different classifications become visible.

Who gets to count: A participant faces the machine across the audit desk, with the comparison between them. The decision record remains in a pending tray as the participant considers the machine’s authority.
A disturbing witness: Return to the two records with the affected lives represented gently beside them. A reader’s hand opens the first report and the book, leaving the judgment unresolved.

visualActionChanges.direction: Present ward and animal facility without graphic injury; contrast care alert and equipment order.
Bring the two reports onto the same desk while keeping their different classifications readable.
Hold the human participant opposite the assessment instrument, emphasizing the question of authority.
End on the comparison sheet and reader hand, leaving both reports unresolved.
